reader_summary:
The section explains why a small fine-tuning change still depends on a large stored model. A few notes added to a thick book do not replace the book. In the same way, this chapter uses an upstream image-text base with pre-existing capability and adds a small candidate LoRA correction. The speech recognizer is a separate dictation component whose output returns to the same chat core, so its contribution has to be evaluated separately. The chapter is not continuing the little chapter-19 MoE by making it bigger.

I can calculate stored weight size from the parameter count and bytes per number. With the stated 2,127,532,032 parameters, four bytes each gives 8,510,128,128 bytes, about 7.93 GiB; two bytes each gives 4,255,064,064 bytes, about 3.96 GiB. This changes storage per number rather than halving the parameter count. Saved computation results, the recognizer and training-update numbers add memory beyond those weights. Dense uses the complete rules rather than selecting experts; selected MoE experts still do not eliminate the storage of all experts. The exercise compares the 328,128-parameter model using the bytes column and asks what is missing for natural photos: appropriate checked picture/answer practice and visible detail, as supplied by the linked training-stage and thin-stroke examples.

The current text explains gradients as numbers used to decide weight changes and optimizer state as extra numbers retained by the update method. These glosses let me explain why the memory estimate omits extra training numbers without first learning optimizer internals.

program_explanation.details: The single Python fence starts with the stated base parameter count. The loop uses the label and bytes_per_number from the two pairs (32-bit, 4) and (16-bit, 2). weight_bytes is their product with parameters. The print line shows exact bytes and an approximate GiB value obtained by division by 1024**3 and rounding to two decimal places. Integer underscores do not change the value. In my notation W = P*b, P is count, b is bytes per number, W is weight bytes; W/1024^3 is GiB. I compared the current code bytes to my actually executed first-round script: they are identical. I reread the preserved actual outputs, which are 8,510,128,128 bytes / 7.93 GiB and 4,255,064,064 bytes / 3.96 GiB. The first run was offline CPU arithmetic in .venv. I did not reexecute in round 2 and did not load or train a model.

The revised text directly warns that the GiB values round to 0.0 and tells me to compare bytes or print more precision, resolving the earlier display obstacle. The current exercise script is byte-identical to the actually executed first-round changed-count script; its preserved outputs are 1,312,512 bytes at four bytes per number and 656,256 bytes at two, both printed as 0.0 GiB. I reuse those real results after exact comparison and did not rerun them. The written answer is supported: natural-picture learning needs suitable images paired with desired checked answers and enough task coverage, plus readable detail preserved by appropriate resolution or windows. Increasing adjustable numbers cannot specify the correct task response by itself or restore a fine stroke already removed by shrinking. Held-out questions check whether the resulting behavior is useful.
